First, the slope of $y=f(x)$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$ is given by ${f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}).$

We will calculate ${f}^{′}(x)$ using the chain rule. First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
f=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(u),\,u=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x).
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(u),\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x).
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡(u)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)) \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we find

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =-3(1)(1) \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find the equation of the tangent at the point $(\frac{\pi }{2},0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-0 & =-3(x-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\ y & =-3x+\frac{3\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$
